title: The Farmer and the Snake
description: Read a complete Greek fable and learn how participles allow Greek to pack a sequence of actions into a sentence.
context: The fables associated with Aesop use short narratives to lead to a moral. In this story, a farmer takes pity on a snake frozen by the winter cold.

grammar.title: The aorist participle
grammar.explanation: An aorist participle often describes an action completed before the main verb. English frequently translates it with 'after', 'when' or by simply coordinating the actions.

example.translation: taking pity on it and picking it up, he placed it...
example.note: The main verb is ἔθετο. The participles explain what the farmer did before placing the snake in his clothing.

grammar.title: A resulting state
grammar.explanation: The perfect can emphasize the state resulting from an earlier action.

example.note: The snake has become frozen or stiff and is found in that resulting condition.

grammar.title: Actions happening together
grammar.explanation: A present participle can describe an action occurring at the same time as the main verb.

example.translation: as he was dying, he said

texts.title: The Farmer Finds the Snake
texts.greek: Γέρων τις γεωργὸς χειμῶνος ὥρᾳ ὄφιν εὑρὼν ὑπὸ κρύους πεπηγότα, τοῦτον ἐλεήσας καὶ λαβὼν ὑπὸ κόλπον ἔθετο.
readingHints: Find the main verb first: ἔθετο.
The subject is γέρων τις γεωργός: 'a certain old farmer'.
εὑρών, ἐλεήσας and λαβών are participles describing actions leading up to ἔθετο.
Do not try to preserve the Greek participial structure mechanically in English.
texts.translation: An old farmer, finding during winter a snake stiff with cold, took pity on it, picked it up and placed it in his bosom.

texts.title: The Snake Revives
texts.greek: Θερμανθεὶς δὲ ἐκεῖνος καὶ ἀναλαβὼν τὴν ἰδίαν φύσιν, ἔπληξε τὸν εὐεργέτην καὶ ἀνεῖλε.
readingHints: The main verbs are ἔπληξε and ἀνεῖλε.
Θερμανθείς means that the snake has been warmed.
ἀναλαβών describes what happens before the main actions.
τὸν εὐεργέτην is the object of the snake's attack.
texts.translation: But when it had been warmed and recovered its natural character, it struck its benefactor and killed him.

texts.title: The Farmer's Last Words
texts.greek: θνήσκων δὲ ἔλεγε· «δίκαια πάσχω, τὸν πονηρὸν οἰκτείρας.»
readingHints: θνήσκων and ἔλεγε happen at the same time: 'as he was dying, he said'.
δίκαια πάσχω is literally something like 'I suffer just things'. Look for natural English.
οἰκτείρας gives the reason for his fate: he pitied a wicked creature.
texts.translation: As he was dying he said, 'I suffer justly for having pitied the wicked.'

texts.title: The Moral
texts.greek: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ, ὅτι ἀμετάθετοί εἰσιν αἱ πονηρίαι, κἂν τὰ μέγιστα φιλανθρωπεύωνται.
readingHints: ὁ λόγος here refers to the fable or story.
δηλοῖ introduces what the story demonstrates.
ὅτι introduces the content of that lesson.
texts.translation: The story shows that wicked natures do not change, even when they are treated with the greatest kindness.
